decisions.quote: We conducted four replications of Shackelford and colleagues (2004). We replicated the effect that males are more distressed by sexual infidelity than females in younger samples but we observed an effect size 50% of Shackelford et al’s original studies (their d = 1.04, our Md = .52). We did not replicate the effect in older samples. Both our effect being smaller and the effect not replicating in older samples were confirmed in our meta-analysis.
decisions.reason: Shackelford et al. (2004) tested sex differences in distress from infidelity in early adulthood and in later life (with the older-adult sample being the primary new data in the 2004 paper). Across four replication studies (Studies 1, 2, and 4 with younger adults; Studies 3 and 4 with older adults), the authors explicitly report that they replicated the sex difference in younger samples (with a smaller effect size) but did not replicate the effect in older samples. In the abstract they summarize the four replications as having 'found different results' (finding the sex difference in younger samples and no effect among older samples), and in the discussion even their statement that the findings 'can be considered a successful replication of the original results with two important qualifications: Size of the effect and whether the effect extends to older adults' explicitly qualifies the replication by the failure of the older-adult finding to replicate. Because a central tested finding of the original study failed to replicate while the younger-adult finding replicated, the shipped 'mixed' outcome is supported and not an error.
